title: Mechowodt Treaty and Reserved Rights Landscape, 1639
summary: A 1639 Dutch agreement associated with Mechowodt of the Massapequa/Marossepinck world describes Native people reserving rights to remain on the land, plant corn, fish, hunt, and make a living there.
address_label: South shore landscape, Rockaway-to-Suffolk treaty context
ancestral_territory_note: Linked to Merrick Ancestral Land as part of a broader south shore diplomatic and land-rights context involving overlapping Native polities.
why_this_matters: The Mechowodt agreement complicates simple stories of land "sale." It shows Native leaders negotiating continued use and presence, and it helps explain how colonial legal records could both preserve Native claims and become instruments of dispossession.
introduction_title: Reserved Rights in a Colonial Record
introduction_content: The Freeport/Merrick south shore helps explain a broad legal landscape and the difference between Native land-use rights and colonial ownership claims.
